title: The Analytics on Prod

scenario.situation: Customer-facing app latency has spiked. Engineering traces it to the production PostgreSQL database being hammered by long-running analytics queries from the BI team.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: The engineering lead believes the fix is to rewrite the slowest queries and add more read replicas to the primary database.
scenario.question: Is query tuning and scaling the primary database the right solution — or is something more fundamental wrong?

decisions.prompt: The engineering lead wants an answer fast. How do you frame the investigation?

options.label: Profile and rewrite the slowest queries
options.detail: Pull EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the top-10 slowest queries and look for missing indexes or bad query plans.
options.consequence: You find a few missing indexes and shave some time off individual queries. But the underlying full-table scans still lock rows and compete with OLTP writes. The app is still slow under any reporting load.
options.divergenceCost: Anchored on the symptom (slow queries) rather than diagnosing why those queries are structurally expensive on this engine.

options.label: Workload characterization across query types
options.detail: Classify all database queries by workload type — transactional (point reads/writes) vs analytical (aggregations, full scans) — and measure their resource footprints separately.
options.consequence: You immediately see two completely different access patterns sharing one engine. Analytical queries touch millions of rows; transactional queries touch a handful. That mismatch — not any single query — is what saturates I/O and blocks OLTP.

options.label: Benchmark vertical scaling options
options.detail: Model how much latency improves if you double CPU and RAM on the primary database instance.
options.consequence: A bigger instance reduces contention temporarily, but analytics scans grow with data volume. You've bought months, not a fix. Costs rise; the problem returns.
options.divergenceCost: Jumped to a capacity solution before confirming whether the architecture — not the hardware — is the root cause.

options.label: Add read replicas and route BI traffic there
options.detail: Spin up PostgreSQL read replicas and point the BI tool at them instead of primary.
options.consequence: Replication lag causes BI reports to reflect stale data, and full-table scans on a row-store replica are still slow — the workload mismatch is unchanged. You've moved the problem, not solved it.
options.divergenceCost: Treated a row-store replica as an analytics tier without questioning whether row-store is the right engine for the workload.

decisions.prompt: Workload classification is done. Which metric do you use to show where the contention really lives?

artifact.title: Total query execution time by query type — last 7 days (hours)
artifact.caption: Raw cumulative execution hours. BI queries dominate total time — but is that because there are more of them, or because each one is intrinsically expensive on a row-store?

options.label: Total cumulative execution time per query type
options.detail: Sum all execution hours for each query class over the past week.
options.consequence: BI queries look catastrophic — but there are far fewer of them than OLTP queries. You might conclude BI is simply more popular, missing the structural cost per query entirely.
options.divergenceCost: Compared raw totals across query classes with wildly different volumes — size confounds the signal.

options.label: Median execution time per query, by type and rows scanned
options.detail: Normalize by query count and plot median latency against rows touched for each query class.
options.consequence: Normalized, the picture is stark: a single BI aggregation touching 5M rows takes 40× longer than a thousand OLTP point reads combined. The cost isn't frequency — it's that sequential row-by-row scans are the worst-case workload for a row-store engine.

artifact.title: Median query latency by type (seconds per query)
artifact.caption: Per-query, BI full-table scans are 2,500× slower than OLTP reads — a mismatch that no index or replica can fully paper over on a row-store engine.

decisions.prompt: Per-query latency shows BI scans are structurally expensive on the row-store. What do you tell the engineering lead?

options.label: "Query tuning won't fix this — move all analytics to a columnar store immediately."
options.detail: Make the architectural call and push for immediate migration.
options.consequence: The recommendation is directionally right, but without a proof-of-concept you can't rule out that ETL latency, schema translation costs, or BI tool compatibility introduce new problems. Acting without a validation step risks a costly migration that trades one set of issues for another.
options.divergenceCost: Overclaimed certainty and skipped the validation step that would de-risk the architectural change.

options.label: "The data shows a fundamental workload mismatch, not a query quality problem — columnar OLAP is the structural fix, but let's run a focused pilot before full migration."
options.detail: Present the workload evidence, name the architectural solution, and recommend a time-boxed pilot on a columnar store with a representative query sample before committing.
options.consequence: The engineering lead sees the evidence, understands why tuning is a local fix to a global problem, and greenlights a pilot. The pilot confirms the columnar store reduces BI query latency by over 90% with zero impact on OLTP — making the migration decision defensible and low-risk.

insight: The app slowdown wasn't caused by poorly written queries — it was caused by running an analytical workload on an engine designed for transactional point access. Row-store engines sequentially scan every column in every row even when only one column is needed, making full-table aggregations structurally expensive regardless of indexing. The lesson is architectural: OLTP and OLAP are different workloads that belong on different engines, and no amount of query tuning or hardware scaling changes the fundamental mismatch.
